title: Kind to everyone
hookLine: if someone despises me, that's theirs; mine is to be kind to all (Meditations 11.13)

lines: WIN THEM, OR DISLIKE THEM BACK?
cards: There's someone who doesn't like you. A relative, a neighbor, a coworker who rolls their eyes when you talk.
It's tempting to make it a project: win them over, dislike them right back, or make sure everyone knows who started it. Marcus asks it plainly in book eleven: does someone despise me?
Then he splits the problem neatly in two, and keeps only one half.

teach.b: First, the split. Does someone despise me? Marcus writes.
That's for them to see to. Mine is to make sure I'm not found doing or saying anything that deserves contempt. Does someone hate me?
Mine is to be gentle and kind toward everyone, this person included. Second, ready to show them.
He adds that he'll be ready to show that very person where they've gone wrong, not by scolding, and not by making a show of his own patience, but nobly and honestly. Third, Phocion.
He gives an example: like the great Phocion, unless Phocion was only pretending. Phocion was an Athenian general condemned to death by his own city.

Plutarch tells that before he died, someone asked whether he had a message for his son, and he said to tell him to bear no grudge against the Athenians. Marcus admires it, then adds a dry footnote: unless it was an act.

teach.h: A WEEK OF DRAWING THE LINE.
teach.b: Fourth, the week, looking back. As on a mountain. Is it this.
Let it be false. Lightly. My own fruit.
And now, theirs, and mine. Several of them draw a line between what belongs to others and what belongs to you, and put your effort on your own side of it. Their opinion is theirs.

how: People who draw on this passage often separate another person's dislike from their own conduct, checking whether they've given real cause, and then offering ordinary kindness regardless.

o: a Spartan king who forgave the men who exiled him
an Athenian general who asked his son to bear no grudge
a Roman senator who refused to judge Marcus harshly

games.q: kind to everyone — tap the pairs.

s: Marcus tells himself to win over everyone who dislikes him
he says their contempt is their concern; his is to be kind and blameless.
he holds up Phocion as an example, with a footnote that it might have been an act
like the great Phocion, he writes, unless he was only pretending.

games.q: someone hates you. you're Marcus. what's your half of it?
o: make sure they know they started it.
be gentle and kind toward everyone, them included.
games.why: their hatred is theirs to see to, he writes. his part is to be gentle and kind to all, and ready to show the person their mistake, without scolding.

practice: Picture someone who dislikes you, and divide the space between you: on their side, their opinion of you, which you can leave there; on your side, your own words and actions.
Ask honestly whether anything you did deserves their contempt. Then choose one small kindness you could offer them, plainly, with no show.

wordCard.voice: Phocion. The Athenian general condemned by his own city, who asked that his son bear no grudge against the Athenians. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: theirs, and mine. Seven days of books ten and eleven, done. Rest easy.
